title: Measure Zero And Sard's Theorem
notes: Open the appendix as the analytic engine behind regular values. The audience should leave this first slide knowing that measure zero is a quantified cover condition, while Sard says the values created by rank failure form an exceptional set too small to obstruct generic choices.

title: From Covers To Regular Values
notes: Use the route as a proof map rather than a theorem list. Each stop adds one type of budget: first box volume, then slice length, then Lipschitz inflation, then critical set decomposition, and finally Taylor decay for the hard layers in Sard's proof.

title: Measure Zero Is A Cover Budget
notes: Stress the quantifier order in the definition. The rectangles may depend on epsilon, and there is no requirement that the cover be efficient or unique. What matters is that every positive volume budget can be beaten by a countable rectangular cover.

title: Null Covers Survive Refinement
notes: Use the shrinking tube picture to explain why low dimensional sets can be invisible to ambient volume. A curve in the plane is not small because it has short length; it is small because its tubular cover can be narrowed until the total area is below any target.

title: Fubini Reads Thinness By Slices
notes: Present Fubini as a way to turn many one dimensional estimates into one ambient estimate. The slide is deliberately schematic: if vertical sections have tiny total length for most x values, integrating those lengths gives an area bound for the whole set.

title: Smooth Images Need Compact Control
notes: The important local hypothesis is compactness of the coordinate patch. On such a patch, bounded derivatives give a Lipschitz constant, so each small box maps into a controlled enlarged box. The source budget is multiplied, not destroyed, by the smooth map.

title: Critical Values Are Images Of Rank Failure
notes: Separate three spaces that students often merge: the domain point, the derivative at that point, and the value in the target. A point is critical when the derivative loses rank; a value is critical only if at least one critical point maps to it.

title: Fold Model: Rank Drops Along A Line
notes: The fold is the simplest local warning sign. Its critical set is a clean line in the domain, and its critical values lie on a clean line in the target. This example makes the theorem believable without pretending that every critical image is so orderly.

title: Cusp Model: Critical Images Can Bend Sharply
notes: The cusp keeps the same diagnostic structure while making the image more singular. The derivative determinant cuts out a parabola in the domain, and mapping that parabola produces a pointed curve in the target. Sard measures this curve by ambient area, not visual complexity.

title: Mini-Sard Works In Local Coordinates
notes: Frame the proof strategy as localization plus bookkeeping. Charts reduce the problem to Euclidean boxes, compact pieces make derivative bounds finite, and the critical set is sorted by how much derivative information vanishes. The theorem is then assembled from countably many null pieces.

title: Taylor Decay Beats Cube Counting
notes: This is the quantitative heart of the argument. A cube of side r has many neighbors, but if enough derivatives vanish, the image diameter shrinks like a higher power of r. The exponent inequality records exactly when the volume budget tends to zero.

title: Sard Proof Scaffold
notes: Use the dependency graph to keep the analytic lemmas from feeling disconnected. Null covers and Fubini establish the language of small sets, smooth image control moves smallness through maps, and the Taylor layer estimate handles the critical set that remains.

title: Manifold Measure Zero Is Chart Local
notes: The manifold definition is not a new measure theory; it is Euclidean measure zero transported through charts. Compatibility matters because smooth transition maps preserve the null condition on compact subpatches, letting the statement survive changes of coordinates.

title: Why Differential Topology Keeps Using Sard
notes: Connect the appendix back to the main course. Regular values give submanifolds, transversality arguments need avoidable bad values, and degree or intersection constructions often require choosing a value away from a thin exceptional set. Sard supplies the permission to choose generically.

title: Inspection Checklist
notes: Close with a usable diagnostic checklist. When students meet Sard later, they should ask which map is being studied, where its derivative drops rank, how the critical image is localized, and why the bad values form a null set rather than merely a visually small set.
